_comment: Declared, reasoned differences between packages/tar and Python's tarfile. Every entry must say WHY. Two things are never declarable: sourcesAgree:false (the package contradicting itself), and a crash.
_format: Keys are 'policy:stricter-than-python' (a blanket policy, see below), 'lenient:<basename>' (we accepted an archive Python refused -- the dangerous direction, declarable only per archive), 'count:<basename>' (entry counts differ), or 'name:<ours>:<theirs>'.
policy:stricter-than-python: We refuse archives that Python's tarfile recovers from. Tar has no index and no terminator it can rely on, so a reader meeting a damaged header has to choose between stopping and skipping ahead to look for the next plausible one; Python skips, we stop. POSIX.1-2017 specifies the layout of a well-formed archive and does not require a reader to resynchronise after damage, so both readings are permitted and this is a policy choice rather than a defect. The choice is to stop, because a reader that resynchronises is deciding on the user's behalf which parts of a corrupt archive to trust -- and tar records no checksum over an entry's CONTENTS, only over its header, so there is nothing left to catch a wrong guess. The strictness is only ever in the safe direction: the opposite case, where we accept something Python refuses, is NOT covered by this policy and fails the diff per archive.
policy:name-encoding-unspecified: Tar records no character set for an entry name, so a name whose bytes are not valid UTF-8 has no single correct presentation and two readers legitimately render it differently. Python uses surrogate escapes (each undecodable byte becomes U+DC80+byte); we map such a name through Latin-1, which is what most tools in practice do and what keeps every byte recoverable. The BYTES agree -- only the rendering differs -- and POSIX.1-2017 pax specifies the field as bytes without an encoding, so neither reading is wrong. Declared narrowly: the comparison is skipped only when Python's own name contains a surrogate escape, which is exactly the not-valid-UTF-8 case. A name where both readers produced valid text and still disagreed still fails.
policy:python-stops-early: On some damaged archives we list MORE entries than Python. Python's tarfile stops walking at the first header it dislikes and returns the members it has so far, rather than raising -- so its listing is silently short. Verified independently rather than assumed: a third checksum walk, written in the diff harness and belonging to neither implementation, found 9 headers with VALID checksums and 0 bad in the archives where Python reported 1 or 3 members, and the 6 entries we list are exactly the 6 the undamaged archive holds (the other 3 headers are the extended pseudo-entries bsdtar writes, which are consumed rather than listed). We are reading these archives correctly and Python is giving up early. Declared in one direction only: listing more than Python is covered, listing FEWER is never covered, because that would mean we are the ones missing entries.
